notes.meaning: Abraham was now about 140 years old, having lived a long life full of severe trials and rich blessings from God. The Lord had granted him wealth, honor, and a peaceful household in Canaan. His central task now was to pass on God's covenant promises by securing a godly wife for his son Isaac.

Abraham called his oldest and most trusted servant, most likely Eliezer of Damascus, who had managed his household affairs for decades. He commanded him to place his hand under Abraham's thigh. In that ancient culture, this was a sacred physical ceremony used to swear an oath of total loyalty and obedience to a master.

Abraham required his servant to swear by the Lord, the true Creator and ruler over both heaven and earth. He strictly forbade Isaac from taking a wife from the surrounding Canaanite tribes. The Canaanites worshiped false gods, and Abraham feared that an ungodly wife would lead his son away from true worship.

Abraham commanded the servant to travel hundreds of miles back to his ancestral homeland in upper Mesopotamia. While Abraham's distant relatives had picked up some pagan practices, they still knew and honored the true God. Marrying within this family ensured Isaac's home would remain faithful to God's covenant calling.

The servant prudently asked for clarity before taking the oath so he would not bind himself to an impossible promise. He wondered what he should do if a woman refused to leave her family and travel to an unfamiliar land. He asked whether he should solve the problem by taking Isaac back to live in Abraham's birthplace.

Abraham immediately gave an emphatic warning never to take Isaac back to that eastern land. Leaving Canaan would mean turning his back on the Promised Land that God had given them. Abraham knew that Isaac had to remain where God called him, even if finding a wife proved difficult.

Abraham reminded his servant that God had originally called him away from that land and had sworn to give Canaan to his offspring. Since God's plan could not fail, Abraham had full confidence that God would send an angel ahead to prepare the way. God's past faithfulness was Abraham's guarantee for the future.

Abraham set his servant's conscience at ease by adding a release clause to the oath. If a young woman refused to accompany him back to Canaan, the servant was completely free from his promise. Yet Abraham repeated his firm instruction that Isaac must never be taken away from the land of promise.

Fully understanding his mission and its limits, the servant placed his hand under Abraham's thigh. He made a solemn promise to the Lord to carry out his master's exact wishes. This quiet act sealed a weighty covenant of duty and trust.

The servant packed a caravan of ten camels with food, travel supplies, and valuable gifts from Abraham's estate. He then set out for the city of Haran in northern Mesopotamia, where Abraham's brother Nahor lived. Having ten loaded camels showed Abraham's great wealth and ensured a proper bridal gift for the woman's family.

Arriving outside the city in the late afternoon, the servant made his camels kneel down to rest by the public well. In ancient towns, drawing water at morning and evening was standard household work done by local women and girls. The servant chose this well so he could discreetly observe the women of the town as they gathered.

Before taking any action, the servant bowed his heart in prayer and asked the Lord for guidance and success. He called on God as the God of his master Abraham, leaning entirely on the covenant faithfulness shown to his master. He trusted that God's quiet providence governed even everyday details.

The servant placed himself in position beside the spring as the young women from the city began coming out with their water jars. He acted with practical wisdom while waiting on God to act. He laid his exact circumstances before the Lord in quiet, expectant faith.

The servant asked God to reveal the chosen bride through a practical test of character. When he asked for a drink, he prayed that the right woman would gladly offer to draw water for all ten of his camels too. Ten thirsty camels could drink dozens of gallons, so this sign looked for a woman of rare generosity, kindness, and willingness to work hard.

Even before the servant finished his silent prayer, God answered his request. A young woman named Rebekah arrived carrying her water jar upon her shoulder. She was the granddaughter of Abraham's brother Nahor, perfectly fulfilling the kinship requirement Abraham had set.

Rebekah was remarkably beautiful, pure in life, and unmarried. She walked down the stone steps to the underground spring, filled her jar, and carried it back up. Her quiet willingness to do ordinary domestic chores showed her humble and industrious spirit.

The servant hurried forward to meet her and politely asked for a small sip of water from her jar. He asked only for a little water for himself, without mentioning his animals. This left room to see if she would show unusual generosity on her own initiative.

Rebekah responded immediately with warm courtesy, addressing the stranger with the honorable title of my lord. She quickly took the heavy water jar down from her shoulder and held it in her hands so he could drink comfortably. Her quick reaction displayed cheerful and eager hospitality toward a stranger.

After giving him a drink, Rebekah freely offered to draw water for all ten of his camels until they were completely satisfied. Her spontaneous words matched the exact prayer the servant had spoken to God only minutes earlier. Her kindness proved that she was deeply thoughtful and cared for the needs of others.

Rebekah quickly emptied the remaining water into the drinking trough and ran back down the steps to draw more. She repeated this demanding labor over and over until all ten camels had plenty to drink. Her vigorous work showed that her offer was not empty talk, but backed up by energetic effort.

The servant watched her in silent astonishment, amazed at how swiftly and completely God had answered his prayer. He stood quietly, pondering every detail to make sure the Lord had truly made his journey successful. He still needed to discover whether this kind young woman belonged to Abraham's kindred.

When the camels had finished drinking, the servant took valuable gifts from his baggage to reward her for her labor. He presented her with a gold nose-ring and two heavy gold bracelets for her wrists. These rich ornaments showed his heartfelt gratitude and gave proof of Abraham's great wealth.
